ezekiel_passages: 1:5-10 (four-faced cherubim; Ezekiel not named in the passage)
one_line_what_it_says: Irenaeus argues the fourfold Gospel from the four-faced cherubim (lion, calf, man, eagle) on which the Word sits, matching each face to a feature of the Son's work.

work_section: First Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. 8
one_line_what_it_says: Clement cites God's oath 'I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance' (Ezek 33:11) and 'Repent, O house of Israel' (18:30) as the basis for exhorting repentance.
Barnabas reads the promise to take away stony hearts and give hearts of flesh as fulfilled in Christ's coming in flesh, so that the believer's heart becomes a holy temple.
Barnabas applies the river with trees whose fruit gives life (Ezek 47) to descending into the water of baptism full of sins and rising bearing fruit.
Justin quotes Ezekiel 20 to argue that Sabbath and other precepts were given as a sign because of Israel's unrighteousness.
Justin says God's goodness counts as righteous the man who, as Ezekiel tells, repents of sins, and counts as sinful the one who falls from righteousness into ungodliness.
Justin cites God's word through Ezekiel making the prophet a watchman: whoever can speak the truth and does not will answer for the blood of the unwarned.
Jerome says the beginning and ending of Ezekiel are so obscure that, like the start of Genesis, the Hebrews do not study them until age thirty.
Jerome calls Matthew, Mark, Luke and John the Lord's team of four, the true cherubim, using Ezekiel's eyes, sparks, lightning, wheels within wheels driven by the Spirit.
Cyril applies 'I will sprinkle clean water upon you' to baptism, which cleanses the guilty and gives the Holy Spirit.

work_section: Catechetical Lecture 16 (On the Holy Ghost), section 14
one_line_what_it_says: Cyril cites Ezekiel's 'The Spirit of the Lord came upon me and said to me' as proof that the Holy Spirit speaks as a living person.

work_section: Catechetical Lecture 18 (On the Resurrection), heading and section 1
one_line_what_it_says: Cyril opens the lecture on the resurrection with Ezekiel 37:1 and states that the hope of resurrection is the root of good works.
Cyril lists Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel ('I will open your graves') and Daniel as Scripture witnesses to the resurrection of the dead.

work_section: On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 30 (first part)
one_line_what_it_says: Tertullian replies to those who read the dry bones only as the restoration of Israel: the metaphor presupposes a real resurrection of bones.

work_section: On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 30 (second part)
one_line_what_it_says: Tertullian argues that God tested the prophet's faith with 'can these bones live?' before naming Israel, so the vision first reveals the resurrection process and then applies it to the unbelieving people.
Tertullian reads the lament over the king of Tyre as describing the devil, once a good angel, created in Eden and set with a cherub on the holy mountain.
Tertullian says the passage names the author of sin, created irreproachable with free will and afterwards turned to evil by his own choice.
Tertullian reads the mark (Tau) set on the foreheads in Ezekiel as the form of the cross, the sign on Christians' foreheads.
Tertullian says the heavenly Jerusalem of the thousand years after the resurrection is the city that Ezekiel knew and John beheld.

work_section: De Principiis, Book 1, ch. 5, section 4 (first part)
one_line_what_it_says: Origen says Ezekiel's second prophecy to the prince of Tyre cannot be about a man but about a higher power that fell, showing opposing powers were not created evil.

work_section: De Principiis, Book 1, ch. 5, section 4 (second part)
one_line_what_it_says: Origen concludes the 'prince of Tyre' passage refers to an adverse power once holy and happy, fallen when iniquity was found in it.

work_section: De Principiis, Book 3, ch. 1, section 15 (first part)
one_line_what_it_says: Origen states the objection drawn from Ezekiel's promise to take away the stony heart: that nothing lies in our power and all is divine grace.

work_section: De Principiis, Book 3, ch. 1, section 15 (second part)
one_line_what_it_says: Origen replies by analogy of a pupil submitting to a teacher: God removes the stony heart from those who come to Him and receive His teaching.

work_section: De Principiis, Book 4, section 22 (numbering as printed on the page)
one_line_what_it_says: Origen holds that Ezekiel's words on Pharaoh and the prince of Tyre cannot be read of mere men or of the earthly Egypt, and need a spiritual reading.
Origen answers Celsus by comparing Ezekiel's 'The heavens were opened' with the Gospel account of Jesus' baptism, asking why one vision is believed and the other not.
Origen says Ezekiel swallowed the roll at the command of the Logos so that its contents would not be written down for unworthy persons.
Origen says the visions at the end of Ezekiel, with their different gates, obscurely refer to how divine souls enter a better world, alongside the heavenly Jerusalem of Revelation.
Origen cites Ezekiel to show that 'visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children' is not literal: everyone dies for his own sin.

work_section: On Grace and Free Will, ch. 29
one_line_what_it_says: Augustine says the promised removal of the stony heart (Ezek 11:19-20) shows grace does not follow a prior good will, since a heart of stone is the hardest, most inflexible will.

work_section: On Grace and Free Will, ch. 30
one_line_what_it_says: Augustine quotes Ezekiel 36:22-27 to show God acts for His own name's sake, not because of human merit.

work_section: On Grace and Free Will, ch. 31
one_line_what_it_says: Augustine sets 'Make you a new heart' (Ezek 18:31) against 'I will give you a new heart' (36:26): God gives what He commands by helping the one commanded.

work_section: On Grace and Free Will, ch. 32
one_line_what_it_says: Augustine reads 'I will make you to walk in my statutes' (Ezek 36:27) as God making us act by replacing the hard heart with an obedient one.
Augustine cites Ezekiel 20:12, Sabbaths as a sign that God sanctifies, for the eternal Sabbath where our works are seen as His.

work_section: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight), sections 64-65
one_line_what_it_says: Gregory says Ezekiel's charge to the watchmen not to keep silence about vice, and his rebukes of faithless priests and rulers, bear on the pastor's duty.

work_section: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight), section 66
one_line_what_it_says: Gregory summarises Ezekiel's indictment of shepherds who feed themselves and neglect the flock, and God's promise to require His flock at their hands.

work_section: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight), section 112
one_line_what_it_says: Gregory fears hearing 'I will require their souls at your hands' (Ezek 3:18) as a reason pastors dread the office.
Chrysostom says the bishop cannot plead ignorance because, as Ezekiel says, he is set to sound the trumpet; the watchman who fails answers for the blood.
Chrysostom argues that God demands heavier punishment of rulers than of the ruled, and that Ezekiel distinguishes the judgment of the rams from that of the sheep.

father: Cyprian (Roman clergy letter among his epistles)
work_section: Epistle 2 (From the Roman Clergy to the Carthaginian Clergy), section 1
one_line_what_it_says: The Roman clergy warn that shepherds who do not seek the lost, correct the wanderer or bind the broken will be told they have eaten the milk and worn the wool (Ezek 34:3-4).
Cyprian cites Ezekiel 18:20 (the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him) to say no one becomes guilty for another's sin, so sinners can be restored through repentance.
Cyprian cites 'I have no pleasure in the death of him that dies' (Ezek 33:11) as a basis for hope for the repenting lapsed.
Cyprian reads the mark on the foreheads of those who sigh (Ezek 9:4-6) as the sign of Christ's blood, like the blood on the Israelite houses.
